content: Vitamin A, also known as retinol, is an antioxidant that can be synthesized by the human body from beta-carotene. It plays a protective role against solar radiation damage in dark green, yellow, and orange vegetables and fruits, and it is believed to have a similar protective function in the human body. Foods particularly rich in beta-carotene include carrots, squash, broccoli, sweet potatoes, tomatoes (which derive their red color from the compound lycopene), kale, seabuckthorn, collards, cantaloupe, peaches, and apricots. Vitamin C, or ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble compound that serves multiple essential roles in biological systems. Key dietary sources of vitamin C include citrus fruits such as oranges and sweet lime, green peppers, broccoli, green leafy vegetables, black currants, strawberries, blueberries, seabuckthorn, raw cabbage, and tomatoes. Linus Pauling was a prominent advocate for the use of vitamin C. Vitamin E, which includes tocotrienols and tocopherols, is a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects lipids from oxidative damage. Sources of vitamin E include wheat germ, seabuckthorn, nuts, seeds, whole grains, green leafy vegetables, vegetable oils, and fish-liver oil. Recent research has demonstrated that certain tocotrienol isomers possess significant antioxidant properties. Coenzyme Q10 and manganese, particularly in its +2 valence state as part of the enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD), are important vitamin cofactors and minerals with antioxidant functions. Melatonin, a hormone, also exhibits antioxidant properties. Lycopene, a carotenoid terpenoid, is found in high concentrations in ripe red tomatoes. Lutein is abundant in spinach and red peppers. Alpha-carotene and beta-carotene are present in high amounts in foods such as butternut squash, carrots, orange bell peppers, pumpkins, and sweet potatoes. Zeaxanthin is the primary pigment in yellow corn. Astaxanthin, a red pigment, is naturally found in red algae and marine animals higher in the food chain, such as crustaceans and salmon. Canthaxanthin is another carotenoid with antioxidant properties. Flavonoids, a subset of polyphenolic antioxidants, are widely distributed in berries, coffee, and tea. Specific flavonoid subtypes include: Flavones: Luteolin, apigenin, and tangeritin. Flavonols: Quercetin (and related compounds like rutin), kaempferol, myricetin (found in walnuts), and isorhamnetin. Proanthocyanidins, also known as condensed tannins. Flavanones: Hesperetin (metabolized to hesperidin), naringenin (metabolized from naringin), and eriodictyol. Flavanols and their polymers: Catechin, gallocatechin, and their gallate esters; epicatechin, epigallocatechin, and their gallate esters; theaflavins and their gallate esters; and thearubigins. Isoflavones, which are phytoestrogens primarily found in soy, peanuts, and other members of the Fabaceae family, include genistein, daidzein, and glycitein. Stilbenoids: Resveratrol, found in the skins of dark-colored grapes and concentrated in red wine, and pterostilbene, a methoxylated analogue of resveratrol abundant in Vaccinium berries. Anthocyanins: Cyanidin, delphinidin, malvidin, pelargonidin, peonidin, and petunidin. Phenolic acids and their esters also exhibit antioxidant properties. Examples include: Ellagic acid, found in high concentrations in raspberries and strawberries, and in ester form in red wine tannins. Gallic acid, present in gallnuts, sumac, witch hazel, tea leaves, oak bark, and other plants. Salicylic acid, found in most vegetables, fruits, and herbs, but most abundantly in the bark of willow trees, from which it was historically extracted for aspirin production. Rosmarinic acid, found in high concentrations in rosemary, oregano, lemon balm, sage, and marjoram. Cinnamic acid and its derivatives, such as ferulic acid, found in seeds of plants like brown rice, whole wheat, oats, and in foods like coffee, apples, artichokes, peanuts, oranges, and pineapples. Chlorogenic acid, found in high concentrations in coffee (more in robusta than arabica beans), blueberries, and tomatoes. It is produced through the esterification of caffeic acid. Chicoric acid, another derivative of caffeic acid, is found exclusively in the medicinal herb Echinacea purpurea. Gallotannins, hydrolyzable tannin polymers formed when gallic acid esterifies and binds with the hydroxyl group of a polyol carbohydrate like glucose. Ellagitannins, hydrolyzable tannin polymers formed when ellagic acid esterifies and binds with the hydroxyl group of a polyol carbohydrate like glucose. Emblicanins, antioxidant tannins derived from Emblica officinalis. Other non-flavonoid phenolics include curcumin, xanthones, and silymarin (a mixture of flavonolignans extracted from milk thistle), as well as eugenol. Other organic antioxidants include citric acid, oxalic acid, and phytic acid. Lignans, which are antioxidants and phytoestrogens, are found in oats, flax seeds, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, rye, soybeans, broccoli, beans, and some berries. Bilirubin, a breakdown product of blood, has been identified as a potentially significant antioxidant. Uric acid accounts for approximately half of the antioxidant capacity of human plasma.
